title: Why Rich People Drive Old Cars: 15 Money Rules From Real Millionaires
description:
Why do so many real millionaires drive old, boring cars while people with far less money drive brand new SUVs? In this video I go through 15 money rules from real millionaires, from three angles: the car math most people ignore, the psychology of not needing a car to feel successful, and the playbook they apply to everything they buy.

Get The Ryan Rover Money Playbook: [LINK HERE]

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:48 How we got the numbers
2:29 Angle 1: The Numbers
2:36 Rule 1. Let someone else pay the depreciation
4:02 Rule 2. Keep it for ten years or more
5:12 Rule 3. Know the full cost
6:24 Rule 4. Pay cash, or keep the loan short
7:27 Rule 5. Invest the difference
8:39 New every 5 years vs keep it for 10
10:02 Angle 2: The Psychology
10:25 Rule 6. A car is transportation, not identity
11:23 Rule 7. Nobody is watching as much as you think
12:20 Rule 8. Wealth is what you don't see
13:27 Rule 9. Delay gratification
14:43 Rule 10. Escape the hedonic treadmill
15:40 Why rich people care less about status
16:54 Angle 3: The Playbook
17:08 Rule 11. Maintenance beats replacement
18:03 Rule 12. Borrow only for things that grow
18:59 Rule 13. Insure smart
19:59 Rule 14. Automate the good choices
20:47 Rule 15. Spend big on what you love
21:50 How to buy a car the millionaire way
24:00 Your car plan at every stage
25:09 The five most expensive car mistakes
26:16 The old car rule for everything else
27:14 Real people, old cars
28:22 Questions people ask
30:54 Recap: all 15 rules
31:35 What to do next

Sources:
- Thomas J. Stanley, Stop Acting Rich (2009): median price millionaires paid for most recent vehicle about $31,000; The Millionaire Next Door (1996)
- Kelley Blue Book, average new-vehicle transaction price above $50,000 (2025); Edmunds, loan terms and monthly payments
- Carfax and Edmunds, depreciation estimates
- S&P Global Mobility, average age of US light vehicles (record above 12.5 years)
- AAA, Your Driving Costs (more than $12,000 a year to own and operate a new vehicle)
- Morgan Housel, The Psychology of Money (2020): the man in the car paradox
- Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky, The Spotlight Effect in Social Judgment (1999); Mischel, Stanford marshmallow studies, and later replication by Watts, Duncan and Quan (2018)
- Ramit Sethi, I Will Teach You to Be Rich (conscious spending)
- Growth example: monthly compounding at 7% average yearly return (illustration, not a promise)
